idiom_name: hand-written tagged union (flag + union payload) or a bool-returning out-parameter
implementation_notes: C has no option type and no generics over values, so absence lives in a convention rather than in a type. The function-level idiom is the out-parameter with a boolean return (bool parse_int(const char *s, int *out)), which forces the caller to consume the result only after checking; the structurally faithful data-level idiom is a hand-written tagged union - a struct carrying a flag plus a union payload, built by some_*/none_* helpers. The standard defines a union as holding at most one member at a time, so the tag must gate every read. Sentinel returns (NULL, -1, empty string, errno) replace the option per type and conflate 'absent' with 'invalid' or with a legitimate value - exactly the confusion the pattern removes. _Generic (C11) or macro sets can generate one constructor family per type; one struct per payload type is usually less error-prone. The hand-written tagged union IS the C realization of the classic structure, justified exactly when absence must stay distinguishable from an invalid value and NULL is a legal value of the type; where neither holds, the out-parameter convention is the lighter replacement.
pitfalls: A sentinel (NULL, -1, 0) that is also a legal value makes absence undecidable; carry the flag next to the value instead.
Reading a union member other than the one last written reinterprets the bytes; every access must be gated by the tag.
Nothing in the type system stops a caller from discarding the boolean result - the discipline needs review rules or static analysis, not just documentation.
errno is meaningful only directly after a failing call and is not cleared by successful ones; using it as a general absence channel invites stale-value bugs.
